title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: In the short run, the market is a voting machine but in the long run it is a weighing machine.
epigraph.author: Benjamin Graham, as quoted by Warren Buffett

web_blocks.html: Start with what you would actually pay. SoftTech last traded at ₹425.90 on 13 November 2026, up 1.18% on the day, after a verified close of ₹420.95 on 12 November, the last session whose benchmark close was confirmed when I built the ledger [41][42]. On 1,38,42,138 shares outstanding [27] that is an equity value of about ₹590 crore; TradingView shows ₹578 crore because it counts shares slightly differently [41]. Add ₹10.5 crore of net debt (borrowings of ₹32.12 crore plus leases of ₹6.43 crore, less ₹28.06 crore of cash and funds at 30 September 2026 [30]) and the enterprise value, the price of the whole operating business, is about ₹600 crore.

Now set that against what the business earns. Trailing twelve-month consolidated sales are about ₹144 crore and earnings per share ₹3.59, so the stock trades at 119 times earnings, 3.4 times a book value of ₹125 a share, and about 4.1 times sales [37][41]. On operating profit of ₹35 crore the multiple is about 17 times. That last number flatters the stock. Chapter 6 showed that SoftTech capitalised ₹36.5 crore of software development in FY2026, which is 113% of that year's ₹32.2 crore EBITDA [27]. If engineering is a cost of staying in business, as I think it is for a product company, cash earnings before tax were roughly zero. The 17 times is a multiple of a number that has not yet reached shareholders.

The screening tool that feeds this dossier labels the valuation “Reasonable / In-line”. I do not agree, and you should know why. That label compares the multiple with a growth-adjusted band and does not look at return on equity, which is 2.9% [41]. A company that earns 2.9% on shareholders' money and trades at 3.4 times book is asking you to pay for returns it has not yet produced. The multiple is a bet on the years after FY2028, not a description of today.

web_blocks.caption: SoftTech valuation at each March year-end since listing (NSE closing prices; earnings and book value from the consolidated accounts)
web_blocks.takeaway: Prices are NSE closes [42]. EPS, equity and sales come from the consolidated accounts and the price-blind feed [37]. Book value is owners' equity plus reserves divided by shares outstanding at each year-end, my arithmetic.

web_blocks.html: The pattern in that table is the story. Between FY2019 and FY2023 the shares traded at 6 to 36 times earnings while earnings per share fell from ₹7.87 to ₹3.94. From March 2023 to March 2025 the price rose 148%, from ₹142 to ₹352, while earnings per share fell from ₹3.94 to ₹0.95 [42][37]. Nobody paid 371 times earnings in March 2025 because of earnings. They paid for revenue growth, the order book and the promise of a platform. The price then fell 38% over the next twelve months and still closed March 2026 at 61 times a profit that had rebounded. The multiple has behaved like a floating number that follows the mood about growth. Today's 119 times sits in the upper half of its own history.

Here is how the stock got to ₹426. It listed on NSE's SME platform in May 2018 at an issue price of ₹80 [36] and closed its first day at ₹72 [42]. By October 2018 it had fallen to ₹39.50, down 51% from the issue price. The COVID low of ₹34.20 came on 24 March 2020. The shares then climbed to ₹130 in November 2021, ₹197 in September 2022 and ₹266 in October 2023, with a dip to ₹130 in June 2023 along the way. The big move came in 2024, when the price rose 146% from ₹229 in January to an all-time closing high of ₹564.25 on 13 December 2024. In that same month the company issued new shares to Einstein Work and Florintree at ₹405 each [31]. Then came the fall: ₹306 by March 2025 and a low of ₹218.65 on 30 March 2026, 61% below the peak and the deepest drawdown in the stock's history. A 140% rally followed, to ₹525.70 on 18 September 2026, and the price has since given back 20% of it [42].

Put those eight years in one sentence. The shares have returned about 21.7% a year from the ₹80 issue price, 5.3 times the money, against a 139% gain in the Nifty 50 over the same period, but with three separate drawdowns of more than 50% along the way [42]. Realised volatility, the size of the daily swings, is 48% annualised over the last twenty sessions and 40% over sixty, and fifteen of the last 250 sessions moved more than 5% [42]. That is a stock whose price is set by a small and changing group of buyers rather than by institutions that hold through the quarters. The latest shareholding table shows foreign investors at 0.00%, the public, which includes every non-promoter holder, at 81.1%, and 2,355 shareholders in total [37].

Now the question that matters: what does ₹600 crore of enterprise value assume? A reverse discounted-cash-flow model answers it. Instead of forecasting and then valuing, you fix the price and solve for the growth that justifies it. I used a ten-year model with these inputs. Revenue grows at a constant rate for five years, fades to 7% by year ten and then grows 5% forever. EBITDA margin climbs from 25% to a target by year five. Reinvestment, meaning capitalised development plus equipment, falls from today's 27% of revenue to 12% by year eight. Each extra rupee of revenue ties up 35 paise of receivables and working capital. Tax is 27% of EBITDA less reinvestment. Cash flows are discounted at 13%, which is my judgement and not a derived figure: it starts from the 7.08% equity risk premium Damodaran estimates for India [43], and I did not verify a current rupee government-bond yield for this run, so I treat 12% to 14% as a reasonable range for a small, thinly traded company with a long collection cycle. The table shows all three rates.

web_blocks.caption: Revenue growth the current price needs: five-year compound growth from FY2026's ₹132.9 crore, solved so the model equals the ₹600 crore enterprise value
rows: Light (reinvestment falls to 10%, working capital 25 paise per rupee)
web_blocks.takeaway: My ten-year model, run in Python on FY2026 consolidated revenue of ₹132.90 crore [27], enterprise value of ₹600 crore ([41], [30]) and the inputs listed above. It is an illustration of what the price requires, not a forecast.

web_blocks.html: Read the table this way. At a 13% discount rate and a 28% margin, the price needs revenue to compound at 35% a year for five years, from ₹133 crore to about ₹604 crore in FY2031. Even with the friendliest settings in the table (12% discount rate, 32% margin, reinvestment falling to 10% of revenue, working capital at 25 paise per rupee) the requirement is 21% a year, to ₹347 crore. SoftTech grew 39.5% in FY2026 and 20.4% in the first half of FY2027 [27][21], and its own long-range aim is ₹300 crore in three to four years [16]. At the standard settings the price therefore assumes that the company outruns its own plan. At the most generous settings, management's plan is worth up to ₹408 a share, about 4% below the price, so the plan itself is roughly priced in and anything that falls short of it is not.

web_blocks.the_number: The current price needs about 29-35% annual revenue growth for five years at a 28-32% EBITDA margin (13% discount rate), or about 21% at the friendliest settings.
web_blocks.how_calculated: A ten-year free-cash-flow model solved for the growth rate at which the present value of the cash flows equals today's ₹600 crore enterprise value.
web_blocks.the_inputs: FY2026 revenue ₹132.90 crore [27]; reinvestment of 27% of revenue fading to 12%; working capital of 35 paise per incremental rupee of revenue; 27% tax on EBITDA less reinvestment; 5% terminal growth; enterprise value of ₹600 crore from ₹425.90 times 1,38,42,138 shares plus ₹10.5 crore of net debt [30].
web_blocks.the_range: At a 12% discount rate and a 32% margin the requirement is 24.8% (standard) or 21.2% (light settings). At a 14% rate and a 25% margin it is 47.5%.
web_blocks.if_off: If true growth is nearer 20% with a 28% margin, the model is worth about ₹194 a share at 13%. Even the light settings on management's plan give ₹293 to ₹355, below today's price.

web_blocks.html: Take management's own plan at face value: ₹300 crore of revenue in four years, a 22.6% compound rate, at a 28% EBITDA margin [16]. Under the standard settings and a 13% discount rate that is worth ₹222 a share. Under the light settings it is worth ₹293, and with a 12% discount rate ₹355. At a 30% margin the same three values are ₹267, ₹338 and ₹408. Every one of them sits below ₹425.90. The market is already paying for management to hit its target and then some.

A second check uses earnings. If ₹300 crore is reached in FY2030 at a 28% margin, with amortisation near ₹45 crore, earnings per share would be about ₹18.3. At 30 times that is ₹548, a 7.7% annual return over the 3.4 years from today's price. At 40 times it is ₹731, or 17.2% a year. Only the second outcome beats a 13% hurdle, and it needs both the plan to be hit and a premium multiple to survive. SoftTech's history on long-range plans is not encouraging: the February 2024 roadmap promised three times revenue in three years and delivered 2.03 times, and the 25-county US ambition has no disclosed county count to show for it [18][15].

Peers keep us honest. I found no listed Indian company that sells the same permit rule-engine software, so the comparison set is imperfect: Indian software-product and engineering-services companies of similar or larger size, taken from the same-session snapshot [41].

web_blocks.caption: SoftTech and listed Indian software-product and engineering peers: same-session valuation, profitability and technical snapshot
web_blocks.takeaway: These are imperfect peers. The table is a size, multiple and return cross-check, not a like-for-like permit-software valuation; business mixes, customers and growth rates differ.

web_blocks.html: Read ROE and the multiple together. SoftTech's 119 times earnings is 3.7 to 7.3 times the multiples of MapmyIndia (31.7x), Cyient (32.5x), Datamatics (18.9x) and Nucleus (16.4x), and those four earn returns on equity of 17.1%, 7.0%, 14.5% and 11.3% against SoftTech's 2.9% [41]. Only Ramco Systems, at 71 times, trades anywhere near SoftTech's multiple, and its 8.7% ROE and its history, described next, are not a comforting neighbourhood. SoftTech's trailing revenue growth of 35% is three to eighteen times that of the peers, whose growth ranges from 2% to 11%, and that is the one reason a premium is defensible. How large a premium is a judgement call. On return on equity the gap is not close. One caution on the table: TradingView's 8.2% operating margin for SoftTech is measured after depreciation and amortisation, which is why it sits far below the 24-26% EBITDA margin used elsewhere in this report.

web_blocks.mechanism: An Indian software-product company that capitalised product development and carried large trade receivables and unbilled revenue had a very strong share-price run, from ₹68.20 on 22 May 2020 to ₹753.70 on 11 January 2021, an elevenfold gain [42]. After a strategic review of project viability and the recoverability of old receivables, it booked a one-time provision of ₹107.2 crore in Q2 FY2024, part of ₹123.6 crore of provisions on trade receivables and unbilled revenue in the first half [39]. ICRA noted that the company capitalises a significant share of its research and development spend every year [39].
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: The share price fell 74.6%, from ₹753.70 on 11 January 2021 to ₹191.10 on 31 March 2023 [42]. Q2 FY2024 net loss was ₹145.8 crore on operating income of ₹126.8 crore, and ICRA cut the long-term rating to BBB+ (Negative) from A- (Negative) on 8 November 2023 [39]. The FY2024 consolidated net loss was ₹241.9 crore on income of ₹529.9 crore [40].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: A software multiple that rests on bookings and unbilled revenue can last until a provision shows how much of that revenue never became cash. SoftTech reports about ₹53 crore of unbilled contract assets, roughly 40% of gross trade receivables older than a year and a FY2026 credit-loss charge of ₹12.49 crore, bigger than group pre-tax profit [27]. The market's patience for the multiple depends on those lines more than on the order book.

web_blocks.html: Why Ramco rather than a famous global name? Because the mechanism is local and specific: large receivables and unbilled revenue, capitalised product development and a run-up built on growth. SoftTech has all three, on a smaller scale. I am not saying SoftTech will repeat Ramco's provision. I am saying that one larger write-off would remove the earnings that today's price is capitalising, and that the price falls first and the provision follows, as the Ramco dates show.

From the reverse DCF I move to my own forward view. I model FY2028, the year to March 2028, because it is far enough out for the product investments to show up in earnings and near enough to forecast. Revenue, margin, amortisation, interest, other income and tax follow the patterns in Chapters 5 and 6. The value comes from a multiple of earnings in the base and bull cases and a multiple of book value in the bear case, where earnings are negative.

web_blocks.caption: Illustrative FY2028E scenarios (₹ per share) and probability-weighted value
web_blocks.takeaway: Analyst estimates, not company guidance. Interest is ₹4.5, ₹4.0 and ₹3.5 crore, other income ₹2.5, ₹3.0 and ₹3.0 crore, and tax 45%, 35% and 28% in the bear, base and bull cases; EPS uses a 92.7% owners' share of profit and 1.3842 crore shares. All arithmetic was run in Python.

web_blocks.html: Here is the story behind each row. In the bear case collections slip, a JNPA-sized order does not repeat, the German and US subsidiaries keep losing money, and amortisation climbs faster than revenue as the ₹42.7 crore of software under development at September 2026 goes live [30]. The group makes a loss in FY2028 and the stock is valued on its book. In the base case revenue grows about 21% a year, from ₹133 crore to ₹195 crore, the margin holds at the 25.5% of the last three years, amortisation rises to ₹35 crore and the tax rate stays high at 35% because subsidiary losses persist. EPS reaches ₹5.97, two-thirds above today's trailing figure, and the multiple compresses from 119 times to 50 times as growth settles. In the bull case revenue reaches ₹235 crore, a 33% annual rate, as the JNPA order executes, a Middle East permit win lands and the TDR exchange scales; the margin reaches 29%, the tax rate falls to 28% and EPS reaches ₹14.78 at 55 times.

The probability-weighted value is ₹369, 13.5% below ₹425.90. Do not read that as a forecast. Read it as a test of the price. With the bear case held at 30%, the price is fair only if the bull case has a 31% chance instead of 20%. Put another way, today's price already assumes that roughly one outcome in three is the good one, at a time when the three things that would make it good, a second large port or airport order, a first major overseas permit deployment and meaningful TDR volumes, have not yet produced material revenue [21].

Trigger that reopens the valuation work: the audited FY2027 accounts show positive free cash flow after capitalised development (FY2026 was about -₹1.3 crore), or the price falls into the ₹218-₹242 band where the base case alone offers 1.5 to 1 reward-to-risk against a ₹205 stop. Either one changes the numbers in this chapter; nothing else does.

Think of a reverse DCF as asking a landlord what rent a building must earn to justify the asking price. If the landlord says the rent must triple and the tenants must never default, you do not argue about the paint. You ask whether tripling the rent has ever happened in that street. What would I ask the CFO about this chapter? Three things. How much of the ₹36.5 crore capitalised in FY2026 is maintenance of existing products and how much is genuinely new? What portion of the ₹53 crore of unbilled work has been invoiced and collected since March? And at what level of group profit does the tax rate stop being 40% to 77%? The answers decide whether the base case in this chapter is too cautious or not cautious enough.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A price is a set of assumptions you have not written down yet. Here they are: five years of growth near 30%, margins near 28% and a reinvestment burden that halves. None is impossible. All of them together, with no cash return until the early 2030s, is a narrow road. Ask yourself whether you are being paid for walking it.
